title: Cardinal Ops - Concurrency & Streaming Assessment
summary: Initial discovery focused on p95 streaming latency and sustained token/sec throughput across hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer targets: p95 sub-300ms for short streaming responses, steady-state token throughput goals and 200-300 concurrent streaming sessions. Discussed KV cache, burst capacity, VPC and KMS requirements. Agreed to run a focused benchmarking POC and exchange security docs and pricing.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
POC benchmark plan and success criteria
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-09-17 08:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lina Alvarez (CTO - Cardinal Ops), Samir Patel (SRE Lead), Jordan Reyes (Product), Priya Malhotra (Backend)
Shared links: redwood-benchmarking-playbook.pdf (shared), private-deploy-checklist.md (shared), pricing-draft-cardinalops.xlsx (to follow)

[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for carving out time, um this is Maya on the AE side and with me is Ethan our SE. How's that sound?
[00:08] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): Hi Maya, thanks. We've been looking forward to today. We wanted to focus on the real time parts - streaming specifically - and how your hosted offering behaves at scale.
[00:18] Ethan Park (Redwood): Awesome yeah we'll try to be practical. Maybe start with your targets and current infra and we'll map to hosted/dedicated/private options.
[00:26] Jordan Reyes (Product): For context we run an assistant embedded in our trading desk product. Most calls are short — prompt+repl pairs, 40-120 tokens typically, but we also have long-form summarization jobs occasionally (2k-6k tokens).
[00:40] Priya Malhotra (Backend): Our immediate SLO is p95 end-to-end streaming latency under 300 milliseconds for the short flows (<=100 tokens) and for longer streaming we want p95 under 1.2 seconds per 256-token window.
[00:55] Samir Patel (SRE): Concurrency is the other piece — we need to support 200 concurrent streaming sessions during peak, with burst to ~350 for 90s.
[01:08] Maya Chen (Redwood): That's very helpful. Curious what your current stack looks like — are you self-hosting models now or using a cloud LLM API?
[01:16] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): We're currently using a mix; low-volume held-internally for private data features and otherwise using a public API, but latency is inconsistent. We're exploring switching to a provider that can guarantee p95 and give predictable costs.
[01:29] Ethan Park (Redwood): Two quick axes: throughput (tokens/sec) and latency. For streaming short responses p95 is often driven by scheduling and batching on the inference runtime and also by network hops. For Hosted Redwood we have a streaming runtime optimized for continuous batching and prefix caching; for Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools and tuned batching profiles; Private gives you full network proximity but we lose some of our multi-tenant batching gains.
[01:55] Jordan Reyes (Product): Can you unpack 'prefix caching' a bit — we heard about KV cache in your docs but not sure how it affects short streaming calls.
[02:04] Ethan Park (Redwood): Sure. KV cache is the token-level key/value cache for autoregressive decoding. For repeated prompt prefixes — like the system instruction and user history — our runtime can serve those from cache which reduces compute per token and lowers p95. In practice for short calls with a stable prompt template we see 30-60% token compute reduction depending on cache hit rates.
[02:28] Priya Malhotra (Backend): Does that work in Hosted? We worry about cold starts and cache warm-up.
[02:33] Ethan Park (Redwood): Yes in Hosted we maintain warm caches across active model instances — but cold starts happen after idle periods. For Dedicated you can reserve warm pools and avoid most cold starts; and for Private you can pin models to nodes nearby which also reduces cold starts. Cold starts are typically a 100-400ms delta for small models, larger models can be more.
[02:53] Samir Patel (SRE): Ok, so if we need sub-300ms p95 for 40-100 token replies, what are realistic configs?
[03:00] Ethan Park (Redwood): Ballpark: for a 2-3B style model served with optimized kernels and good KV cache hit rate, Hosted can hit p95 ~200-350ms with continuous batching tuned for low-latency; Dedicated with reserved GPUs and lower co-tenancy can push p95 to ~150-220ms. Private on-prem with high bandwidth NICs can be similar to Dedicated but you need the same inference optimizations and kernel builds we supply.
[03:26] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): Those numbers are helpful. We're also very sensitive to token/sec costs — can you share typical tokens/sec throughput per GPU for a medium model?
[03:35] Maya Chen (Redwood): Sure, Ethan do you want to call out numbers?
[03:38] Ethan Park (Redwood): For 8-bit quantized medium family models you'll see roughly 15k-25k tokens/sec per A100-class GPU for streaming workloads when fully saturated; for lower-latency configs we often run at lower saturation which reduces tokens/sec but improves p95. If you need sustained 50k tokens/sec that's where Dedicated pools and autoscale matter — you can stitch more GPUs.
[04:02] Jordan Reyes (Product): We're thinking in user sessions not raw tokens. Each streaming session averages 80 tokens per minute, but we have 200 concurrent sessions at peak so that maps to about 16k tokens/sec?
[04:16] Priya Malhotra (Backend): Quick calc: 200 sessions * 80 tokens / minute = 16k tokens/minute, oh… I think Jordan's unit off.
[04:24] Samir Patel (SRE): Yeah unit check — 80 tokens per minute is low, our session TPS is more like 80 tokens per request with 0.5 req/sec per session during peak — which is about 8k tokens/sec. We should confirm.
[04:37] Jordan Reyes (Product): Sorry my bad — I meant 80 tokens per request and avg 0.5 requests/sec => 8k tokens/sec. So target sustained ~8-10k tokens/sec with bursts to 20k.
[04:48] Ethan Park (Redwood): Great, 8-10k sustained is in the comfortable range for Hosted with autoscale, depending on model family. For predictable throughput and cost you might prefer Dedicated — you get reserved GPUs and can control batching curves.
[05:00] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): What about concurrency per GPU — we want to know how many concurrent streaming sessions a single inference node can handle before latency degrades.
[05:09] Ethan Park (Redwood): That depends on model size and networking. With continuous batching, a single instance can multiplex many sessions; for a medium model on an A100 we often sustain 100-200 concurrent light sessions before p95 starts creeping up. For heavier sessions you partition. Dedicated lets you set higher per-node concurrency ceilings by tuning the runtime.
[05:30] Priya Malhotra (Backend): We're also looking at network topology. If we go Private with VPC peering we need to ensure the KMS integration. Do you support cloud KMS and customer-managed keys?
[05:41] Maya Chen (Redwood): Yes — Hosted supports customer-managed KMS (bring your own key) in our enterprise tiers; Private supports KMS/HSM on-prem integrations. We'll share the security checklist.
[05:51] Samir Patel (SRE): SOC 2 and audit logs — do you provide per-request audit logging with redaction options?
[05:58] Ethan Park (Redwood): Yes we have audit logging options with token-level telemetry in the console; you can redact PII and set retention windows. We'll also send our SOC 2 report and logging doc.
[06:10] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): Ok good. About POC success criteria — we're thinking a 30 minute sustained run at 10k tokens/sec with p95 < 300ms for short responses and demonstration of burst handling to 25k tokens/sec for at least 90 seconds. Is that feasible?
[06:26] Ethan Park (Redwood): Feasible, yes. For Hosted we'll run bench nodes in a dedicated test pool, but for strict isolation we'd recommend Dedicated for the POC. We can run both in parallel to show differences.
[06:36] Jordan Reyes (Product): What tooling do you provide to reproduce our traffic profile?
[06:40] Ethan Park (Redwood): We have a benchmarking harness (we call it the loadprobe) and a recommended test script in the redwood-benchmarking-playbook.pdf. It supports token-level shaping, session emulation, and streaming semantics. We'll provide the harness repo and an infra template.
[06:56] Maya Chen (Redwood): Quick note on costs — Dedicated is more CAPEX-like (committed) but predictable; Hosted is pay-as-you-go and great for ramping. We can model scenarios in the pricing spreadsheet we'll share.
[07:08] Priya Malhotra (Backend): One more question — does your streaming runtime allow for early answer cutoff or delta encoding for smaller payloads? We want to avoid sending full chunks when partials suffice.
[07:19] Ethan Park (Redwood): Yes we support partial flushes and configurable chunk sizes. Delta encoding is something we do in our SDK layer; we can also do server-side trimming if you prefer.
[07:30] [crosstalk]
[07:34] Samir Patel (SRE): Alright, logistics for the POC — we'll need an NDA signed and then a time window to run the sustained test. Our engineering window is next Friday (2027-09-24) morning PST.
[07:45] Maya Chen (Redwood): We can get an NDA over tonight; Ethan can own the bench run.
[07:50] Ethan Park (Redwood): I'll run the 30m 10k sustained with telemetry and then a burst phase. We'll also capture KV cache hit rates and cold start stats and share results.
[07:59] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): What telemetry will you provide post run? We want p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cache hit %, and per-route cost estimates.
[08:12] Ethan Park (Redwood): We'll deliver a benchmark report with those metrics plus flamegraph-style latency breakdowns and operator notes.
[08:20] Jordan Reyes (Product): What's the expected delta between Hosted and Dedicated p95 in your experience?
[08:25] Ethan Park (Redwood): Typically Hosted has slightly more variance; p95 difference is often 50-120ms depending on model and load patterns. Dedicated tightens tail latencies due to resource isolation and deterministic batching windows.
[08:38] Samir Patel (SRE): Any gotchas around tokenization differences or detokenization overhead when comparing models?
[08:44] Ethan Park (Redwood): Good call — tokenization affects tokens/sec math. We'll include tokenizer configs and exact model artifacts in the POC so results are apples-to-apples.
[08:55] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): For Private deployment, what's the timeline to provision a customer instance? We're a few months out but want to know lead time.
[09:02] Maya Chen (Redwood): Private timeline depends on network and compliance work — typically 4-8 weeks for a first private deployment assuming approvals and infra readiness.
[09:12] Priya Malhotra (Backend): Are there any feature differences between Hosted and Private runtimes?
[09:17] Ethan Park (Redwood): Feature parity is our goal; sometimes lower-level kernel builds or cloud vendor drivers in Private need a quick validation pass. We'll run an acceptance test suite.
[09:29] Jordan Reyes (Product): One final ask — can you provide an example sizing recommendation for 8-10k sustained tokens/sec and 200 concurrent streaming sessions?
[09:36] Ethan Park (Redwood): Off the cuff: For a medium-family optimized model, start with 2-3 A100-equivalent GPUs in a Dedicated pool with autoscale to add 2 more on sustained higher load. We'll produce a detailed sizing sheet in the playbook with sample batch curves.
[09:55] Samir Patel (SRE): Cool. Let's wrap with next steps.
[10:00] Maya Chen (Redwood): Recap: Redwood will send NDA and the benchmarking harness, SOC 2 and security checklist, and a preliminary pricing model. We'll schedule the POC bench for 2027-09-24 morning PST and Ethan will run tests and share a report.
[10:15] Lina Alvarez (Cardinal Ops): Sounds good, thank you all.
[10:18] Maya Chen (Redwood): Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and action items.
[10:22] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions present (e.g., "KV cash" appears once), some speaker attribution uncertain in two short segments; overall medium quality.
